hints: Focus on what the two reagents do in sequence, reduction first then dehydration, and what functional groups are present.
Notice that excess NaBH4 reduces both the aldehyde and the ketone, so each starting C7H10O2 compound becomes a diol of formula C7H14O2.
Consider how many different alkenes can form when the secondary ring OH is removed, symmetry makes some eliminations identical and asymmetry makes them different.
walkthrough:
**Reduce both carbonyls with NaBH4**

Both starting molecules contain one aldehyde and one ketone on a cyclohexane ring. Excess NaBH4 reduces aldehydes to primary alcohols and ketones to secondary alcohols.

$$\text{R-CHO} \rightarrow \text{R-CH}_2\text{OH} \quad \text{and} \quad \text{R}_2\text{C=O} \rightarrow \text{R}_2\text{CHOH}$$

**Dehydrate twice with hot concentrated H2SO4**

Heating alcohols with excess concentrated H2SO4 eliminates water to form alkenes. Losing two waters from the diol gives the target formula:

$$\text{C}_7\text{H}_{14}\text{O}_2 - 2\text{H}_2\text{O} \rightarrow \text{C}_7\text{H}_{10}$$

**Check if dehydration gives one or two dienes**

The key is elimination of the secondary ring OH. It can lose H from either neighbouring ring carbon. If those two directions are symmetric, only one cyclohexene intermediate forms. If they are different, two intermediates form and then two isomeric methylenecyclohexene dienes form.

Compound 2 is 1,4-disubstituted and symmetric, so loss of H from C3 or C5 is identical. Compound 1 is 1,3-disubstituted and unsymmetric, so loss of H from C2 versus C4 gives conjugated versus isolated diene isomers.

**Analyse the special 1,2 case**

Compound 3 is 1,2-disubstituted. Loss of the C2 OH with H from C1 gives $\text{C1=C2}$ with $\text{CH}_2\text{OH}$ still on sp2 C1. That C1 then has no H to lose with the primary OH, so it cannot dehydrate a second time to $\text{C}_7\text{H}_{10}$. Only loss with H from C3 leads on to a second dehydration to 3-methylenecyclohex-1-ene. Hence only one $\text{C}_7\text{H}_{10}$ product is possible.

Therefore 2 and 3 give only one final product of formula $\text{C}_7\text{H}_{10}$, while 1 gives two.

options.A: Incorrect. If this option claims 1 alone or includes 1, it is wrong because the 1,3-diol can dehydrate at C3 in two non-equivalent directions to give both the conjugated 3-methylenecyclohex-1-ene and the isolated isomer, so more than one C7H10 product forms.
options.B: Incorrect. Compound 2 alone is incomplete. The 1,4-diol is symmetric and does give only one diene, but compound 3 also gives only one C7H10 product for a different reason, so selecting 2 only misses a valid compound.
options.C: Correct. Compound 2 gives one product by symmetry, and compound 3 gives one product because only one of the two first-elimination routes can undergo a second dehydration to C7H10. Compound 1 gives two isomeric dienes and is excluded.
options.D: Incorrect. Including all three is a trap. It correctly spots that double dehydration gives C7H10 but forgets the 'only one' condition. Compound 1 fails this test because its unsymmetric 1,3 positions allow two different endocyclic alkenes and hence two final dienes.
